analogy.p: Imagine a road trip where at every junction you take one of several roads, each chosen with some probability. A complete journey is a path through the junctions, so its overall chance is the product of the chances of each turn (you must make the first turn and then the second). The chance of reaching one of several destinations is found by adding the chances of the different routes that end there. If a road closure (no replacement) changes which roads are available after a turn, the later probabilities change, which is exactly what happens to the branches in a dependent tree. The analogy breaks down because real junctions are rarely chosen by exact probabilities, and in a tree diagram the probabilities at every junction must add to 1 and are fixed by the problem.

bullets: Each **stage** of the tree is one event (for example the first counter picked, then the second counter picked). Stages run left to right.
Each **branch** represents one possible outcome at that stage. The number written on it is the probability of that outcome **at that stage, given the path taken so far**.
The ends of the final branches are the **outcomes** of the whole experiment (for example red then blue). Writing the outcome and its combined probability at the end makes later questions easy.
At every node (branching point) the branches leaving it must account for **all** the possibilities, so their probabilities add to 1.

Tree diagrams work for both **independent events** (the probabilities do not change) and **dependent events** (the probabilities change because of what has happened, for example picking without replacement).
A tree is a picture of the rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A); this is the heart of the topic.
Trees are most useful when there are two or three stages and each stage has a small number of outcomes.
core.p: A **tree diagram** is a way of listing every possible outcome of two or more events that happen one after the other (in **stages**), and of working out the probability of each outcome. You start at a single point on the left, draw a branch for each possible outcome of the first event, and from the end of each of those branches draw new branches for the second event, and so on. Each branch is labelled with its outcome and its **probability**, and the ends of the final branches list the complete outcomes. The big advantage is that the diagram makes sure you do not miss any outcomes and shows clearly how probabilities combine. For Edexcel Higher tier you must be able to draw, complete and use tree diagrams for independent and dependent events, and use them for conditional probability.

bullets: **Step 1**: decide the stages and the possible outcomes at each stage (for example red or blue).
**Step 2**: from the starting point draw one branch for each outcome of stage 1 and write the probabilities on them (they must add to 1).
**Step 3**: from the end of **each** stage 1 branch draw a full set of stage 2 branches. A common error is forgetting to draw second-stage branches from one of the first-stage ends.
**Step 4**: write the probabilities on the stage 2 branches. If the situation changes after stage 1 (no replacement) the probabilities may be different on different sets of branches.
**Step 5**: at each node check that the probabilities add to 1. If they do not, something is wrong with the numerators or denominators.
**Step 6**: write the outcome at the end of each path (for example RB) and multiply along the branches for its probability.
**Step 7**: check that the probabilities of all outcomes sum to 1. This is a built-in check that catches most slips.
Use a ruler, leave room for fractions, and use fractions or decimals consistently. Do not label branches with ratios or percentages unless the question does.
core.h: Drawing and labelling a tree diagram correctly
core.p: Good tree diagrams are tidy and fully labelled, because marks are given for the shape of the tree, for correct labels and for correct probabilities. Start by identifying the stages and the outcomes at each stage. Draw the branches from left to right with enough space to write probabilities on them. Label every branch with both the outcome and the probability (for example R 3/5), then write the outcome at the end of each complete path. Finally calculate the probability of each outcome by multiplying along the path and write it at the end. In the figure for a bag with 3 red and 2 blue counters picked with replacement, every second-stage set of branches is identical to the first.

bullets: **Multiply along a path** to get the probability of that single outcome: P(RB) = 3/5 × 2/5 = 6/25.
The rule uses the **conditional** probability on the second branch. In the without-replacement figure, P(RR) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 because after one red is taken only 2 reds remain out of 4 counters.
For three stages multiply three numbers: P(R, R, B) = P(R) × P(R | R) × P(B | RR).
Multiplying fractions: multiply numerators together and denominators together, then simplify (3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10).
Multiplying decimals: 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Check the number of decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2.
Probabilities multiplied are always smaller than (or equal to) each individual probability, which makes sense because a sequence of events is harder to achieve than one event.

Why multiply? In 3/5 of all cases the first pick is red; within those cases, 2/4 of the time the second pick is also red. So the fraction of all cases that are RR is a fraction of a fraction: 3/5 × 2/4. A fraction of a fraction always means multiply.
core.h: The AND rule: multiply along the branches
core.p: To find the probability that **both** events happen (or that a complete sequence of events happens), you **multiply** the probabilities along the branches of the path. This works because the second probability on the path is already the probability of the second event **given that the first has happened**. In symbols, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A). For independent events, P(B | A) is just P(B), so P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). In the figure with replacement, P(red then red) = 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25. A useful way to remember it: the word 'and' (or 'then') means multiply and goes along a path.

bullets: Identify **every outcome (end of a path)** that satisfies the question, for example 'same colour' = RR and BB.
Calculate the probability of each of those outcomes by multiplying along its path, then **add** the results. Example (with replacement): P(same colour) = 9/25 + 4/25 = 13/25.
Without replacement: P(same colour) = 6/20 + 2/20 = 8/20 = 2/5.
Never add probabilities along a branch and never multiply the outcome probabilities at the ends together.
Outcomes at the ends of a tree are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so their probabilities add to 1. If your list of outcomes does not, there is an error.
Write the outcomes you are using, for example 'RB or BR', before adding. This shows the examiner which paths you chose and gains method marks.
Exactly one red means RB or BR but not RR or BB: be careful to distinguish 'exactly one' from 'at least one'.
core.h: The OR rule: add the outcome probabilities
core.p: Often a question asks for the probability of an event that can happen in **more than one way**, for example 'the two counters are the same colour' (RR or BB) or 'exactly one red' (RB or BR). Each way is a separate path through the tree, and the different outcomes are **mutually exclusive** (they cannot both happen). So you find the probability of each relevant path by multiplying along it, and then **add** those path probabilities together. The word 'or' means add and joins different paths. This is why the tree is organised as it is: multiply along branches, add between outcomes.

bullets: **With replacement** means the item is put back, so the total and the numbers of each colour are unchanged for the second pick.

Examples of independent events: successive coin tosses, rolling a die, spinning a spinner, picking with replacement, and events involving different people not affecting each other (assumption stated).
In exam questions, look for phrases such as 'replaced', 'put back', 'independent', 'each time' or 'two separate spins'.
The probabilities on a given set of branches always add to 1, e.g. 3/5 + 2/5 = 1.
The probability of the **same outcome** twice, for example two sixes on a fair die, is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.
For n independent identical events the probability of all n is (p)ⁿ: for three heads, (1/2)³ = 1/8.
State any **assumptions** when asked: 'the events are independent', 'the coin is fair', 'the selection is random'.
Independence is a property of the situation; it does not depend on the answer. Do not call events independent if the second probability changes.
core.p: Two events are **independent** if the outcome of the first does not affect the probability of the second. A classic example is taking an item and **replacing** it before taking the next one, tossing a coin twice or rolling a die twice. In a tree diagram for independent events the second-stage branches repeat the first-stage probabilities and are the same on every branch. For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). In the first figure (3 red and 2 blue counters, with replacement), each pick has P(R) = 3/5 and P(B) = 2/5 because the bag returns to its original state each time.

bullets: **Always reduce the denominator by one** each time an item is removed: 5, then 4, then 3, and so on.
**Reduce the numerator** only for the colour (or type) that was removed. After removing a red from 3R 2B the red numerator drops from 3 to 2, but the blue numerator stays 2.
The second-stage probabilities are **conditional probabilities**: P(red on 2nd | red on 1st) = 2/4.
Words signalling no replacement: 'without replacement', 'not put back', 'takes two sweets and eats them', 'two students are chosen' (cannot be chosen twice).
Watch for a hidden change: if a question says 'at random, two are chosen', assume without replacement unless told otherwise.
Common error: leaving the second-stage probabilities the same as the first-stage ones when items are not replaced. Make a habit of writing the new contents of the bag next to each branch set.
core.h: Dependent events and selection without replacement
core.p: Two events are **dependent** if the outcome of the first changes the probability of the second. The most common situation is picking items **without replacement**: when an item is removed, both the **total number** and possibly the number of that type decrease. On the tree this means that the second-stage branches have different probabilities depending on which first-stage branch you followed. In the second figure, a bag has 3 red and 2 blue counters and two are taken without replacement. After a red is taken, 2 red and 2 blue remain (4 counters). After a blue is taken, 3 red and 1 blue remain (4 counters). The branch probabilities at each node still add to 1.

bullets: **P(B | A)** is read directly off the second-stage branch that follows A. It is not found by multiplying anything.
The conditional probability P(B | A) is not the same as P(A and B). The 'and' probability multiplies the first-stage probability and the conditional one: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B | A).
If the events are independent then P(B | A) = P(B): knowing A has happened makes no difference. In a tree, the second-stage probabilities are then the same on every branch set.
In words: 'Given that it rained, the probability of being late is 0.4'. Examiners reward the correct wording of the given condition.
Typical signal words: 'given that', 'if', 'of those who', 'knowing that', 'what proportion of ... also ...'.
The first-stage probabilities on a tree are unconditional (for example P(rain) = 0.3).
Some questions give the conditional probabilities in a table or sentences and ask you to complete the tree. Read each sentence carefully to put numbers on the correct branches.
core.p: **Conditional probability** is the probability of an event **given that** another event has already happened. It is written **P(B | A)**, read 'the probability of B given A'. The vertical bar means 'given that'. A tree diagram makes conditional probabilities easy to see, because the probabilities on the **second-stage branches** are conditional probabilities: they depend on which first-stage branch you took. In the weather example (rain 0.3; late 0.4 if raining; late 0.1 if dry), the branch labelled late 0.4 after rain is P(late | rain) = 0.4, while the branch late 0.1 after dry is P(late | dry) = 0.1. Different conditions produce different probabilities.

bullets: **Step 1**: write what you want in the form P(A | B) and identify the given event B ('late').
**Step 2**: find P(B) by **adding all paths that end in B**. P(late) = 0.3 × 0.4 + 0.7 × 0.1 = 0.12 + 0.07 = 0.19.
**Step 3**: find P(A and B), the path where both happen: P(rain and late) = 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12.
In words: out of all the late outcomes (0.19 of the total), the proportion that came from rain is 12 out of 19.
Notice that P(late | rain) = 0.4 is not the same as P(rain | late) = 12/19. Do not swap them.
Using **frequencies** can help: imagine 1000 days. Rain and late: 120; dry and late: 70. Late days = 190. Of those, 120 were rainy: 120/190 = 12/19.
The denominator is **not 1** and **not the first-stage probability**. It is the total probability of the given event.
core.h: Reversing the condition: finding P(A | B) from a tree (Higher tier)
core.p: A harder Higher tier question gives a tree built in one order (for example weather then lateness) and asks for a conditional probability in the **opposite order**, such as 'given that Sam was late, what is the probability that it rained?'. You cannot read this directly from a branch. Instead use **P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B)**. The numerator is the probability of the single outcome 'rain and late' (a path), and the denominator is the **total probability of the given event** 'late' which is found by adding **all** the outcomes in which Sam was late. This works because, once you know Sam was late, the only outcomes still possible are the late ones, so the probability becomes the fraction of those that involve rain.

bullets: **P(at least one red) = 1 − P(no red)**. Without replacement, 3R and 2B, two taken: P(BB) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 1/10, so P(at least one red) = 1 − 1/10 = 9/10.
With replacement the same event is 1 − (2/5)² = 1 − 4/25 = 21/25.
'At least two' needs adding paths (or the complement 'zero or one'), so check which route is shorter.
**'None'** means every stage fails. For independent events, P(none) is the product of the individual failure probabilities, e.g. at least one six in three rolls = 1 − (5/6)³ = 91/216.
**'At least one' is not the same as 'exactly one'**. Exactly one is a sum of selected paths (RB + BR) and does not include RR.
In an exam, write 'P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)' as a line of working. It shows the method.
If you add the paths instead of using the complement you must include every path with at least one; leaving one out is a common error.
core.h: 'At least one' questions and using the complement
core.p: Questions asking for the probability of **at least one** of something are usually quickest using the **complement**: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none). 'At least one red' covers every outcome except 'no reds', which is a single path (for two stages, BB). Instead of adding several outcomes (RR, RB and BR) you find one and subtract from 1. The method comes from the fact that the probabilities of all outcomes add to 1, so the event and its complement account for everything. This approach becomes essential for three or more stages where the number of outcomes grows quickly (a three-stage tree has 8 paths).

bullets: For three stages with replacement, P(R, R, R) = 3/5 × 3/5 × 3/5 = 27/125.
Without replacement: P(all three milk) from 5 milk and 3 dark = 5/8 × 4/7 × 3/6 = 60/336 = 5/28. The denominators go 8, 7, 6 and the milk numerator goes 5, 4, 3.
The number of paths is (outcomes per stage)^(stages). Sketching only the needed paths avoids a huge diagram, but label them clearly.
For 'exactly one' in three stages there are 3 arrangements (for example RBB, BRB, BBR). Each has the same probability if events are independent, so P = 3 × p × q × q.
Always check that your outcome probabilities add to 1 if you draw the full tree.
Three-stage conditional probabilities use the same formula P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B); the numerator and denominator may each need several paths.
Keep a clear layout: leave enough vertical space and put the probabilities close to their branches.
core.p: Some questions need three stages, for example choosing three items or three days of weather. A three-stage tree has 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 paths if each stage has two outcomes, so it is long to draw in full. The same rules apply: multiply along branches, add the relevant paths. When only particular outcomes are needed you may be allowed to draw only the **relevant branches** (a partial tree) to save time, but only when the question asks for a single outcome or a simple combination and you are sure to label clearly. The key habit is to keep updating the numbers after each removal in a without replacement question, and to give each branch a clear label.

bullets: Frequency tree example: 200 people, 60 % commute by car. Car = 120, other = 80. Of the car users 25 % are late: 30; of the other 10 % are late: 8. Total late = 38.
Conditional probability from the frequency tree: P(car | late) = 30/38 = 15/19. You simply use the numbers.
**Expected number** = probability × number of trials. If P(late) = 0.19 and there are 100 days, expected late days = 0.19 × 100 = 19.
An expected value is an average over many trials and is not a guarantee. It need not be a whole number (for example 18.5).
In a frequency tree, the numbers at each split must add up to the number before the split. Use this to check.
To convert a frequency tree to probabilities, divide each branch number by the number at the node it came from.
Use frequency trees when the question gives counts, percentages of groups or says 'out of 200'.
core.p: A **frequency tree** is a tree diagram that shows **numbers of items** instead of probabilities. You start with the total (for example 200 students) and split it at each branch into the numbers in each category. Frequency trees are often easier to understand than probability trees, especially for conditional probability, because you are working with whole numbers and can see directly how many are in each group. Expected frequencies from a probability tree are found by **multiplying the probability by the number of trials**: expected number = probability × n.

bullets: **Tree diagram** best for sequences, replacement or no replacement, and conditional probability by branches.
**Venn diagram** best for groups with overlaps and 'both', 'either', 'neither' language; conditional probability by restricting to a circle.
**Two-way table** best when data are classified two ways (for example year group and trip choice); conditional probability by a row or column total.
Common assumptions to state: 'the events are independent', 'the coin is fair so P(head) = 0.5', 'each item is equally likely to be chosen'.
If a probability tree gives P(A | B) ≠ P(A), say 'the events are not independent' with the numbers as evidence.
Give a comment if asked 'is this model realistic': for example, weather on consecutive days is usually not independent, because wet days tend to follow wet days.
Do all arithmetic carefully, and keep exact fractions until the end unless a decimal is needed.
Present your final answer clearly with units or context, e.g. '9/10' or '0.9', and not as a ratio.
core.h: Choosing between trees, Venn diagrams and two-way tables, and stating assumptions
core.p: Tree diagrams are the best choice when events happen **in sequence** or when the second probability depends on the first. Venn diagrams are better for questions about group membership with overlaps, and two-way tables for classifying a population by two features. In many Higher tier problems you can solve with more than one representation, which is a useful way to check an answer. Whichever you use, examiners expect you to state any **assumptions** when asked: that events are independent, selections are random, or a coin or die is fair. The mark schemes also expect probabilities to be written as fractions, decimals or percentages, and simplified if the question says 'give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form'.

bullets: Write the product for each path you use, for example 3/5 × 2/4, even if you use a calculator. Method marks depend on it.
Use the **sum to 1 check** at every node and at the end of the tree. If a probability is missing, find it by subtraction (1 − the others).
Convert between fractions and decimals consistently; do not mix 3/5 and 0.4 without checking.
'Show that' questions need a full chain of working and a stated final value. 'Give a reason' needs a sentence referring to the context.
Give a fraction in its simplest form where asked; a decimal answer is accepted if exact or correctly rounded to 3 significant figures.
If a question says the probabilities are to be given as decimals use decimals on the tree.
If you are stuck, draw the tree anyway: even a partial tree with correct first-stage branches can earn marks.
Link to the other representations: Venn diagrams use P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) ÷ P(B) too, so the same reasoning transfers.
core.h: Exam technique: layout, checks and common mark schemes
core.p: Tree diagram questions are quite predictable, so a clear routine gains marks. Typical 'complete the tree' questions give 1 mark for each correct set of branch probabilities. 'Work out' questions give 1 mark for a correct method (multiplying along the correct branches), 1 mark for adding the right outcomes and 1 mark for the correct answer. Examiners are very forgiving of untidy diagrams but not of missing working, so always show the products you calculate. Check each answer for sense: probabilities must be between 0 and 1, and an event with more ways of happening should have a larger probability.

exam: **Complete the tree** (1 to 2 marks): fill missing branch probabilities by using 'sum to 1' at each node, and write them in the same form (fractions or decimals) as the question.
**2 mark 'work out the probability of two specific outcomes'**: 1 mark for a correct product (for example 3/5 × 2/4), 1 mark for the answer (3/10). Show the product.
**3 mark 'same colour' or 'exactly one'**: identify the paths (RR or BB), multiply for each, add. Marks: method for each path, then the correct sum.
**3 to 4 mark 'at least one'**: 1 − P(none) is quickest. Write the line 'P(at least one) = 1 − P(none)'.
**Conditional probability (4 to 5 marks, Higher)**: state P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B), find the numerator path, find the denominator by adding all paths in B, divide and simplify.
**Command words**: 'Work out' (calculate, show working), 'Show that' (full working to a stated answer), 'Explain' (a reason in words), 'Complete' (fill in the diagram).
Words that signal **without replacement**: 'not put back', 'takes two', 'without replacing'. Words for **independent/with replacement**: 'replaced', 'each time', 'fair coin'.
A 6 mark question may include several parts: tree completion, a simple probability, then a conditional or 'at least' calculation. Plan by drawing and labelling the tree first.
Give answers as fractions in lowest terms or decimals; do not use ratios or words such as 'likely'. If rounding, state the number of significant figures or follow instructions.
Check: each node adds to 1, all outcomes add to 1, no probability exceeds 1. This takes under a minute and prevents silly errors.
If the question mentions assumptions ('state an assumption'), write 'the events are independent' or 'the selection is random' in a full sentence.

mistakes.r: Without replacement the total goes down by one and the removed type goes down by one: 3/5 then 2/4 for red then red.
mistakes.w: Keeping the same probabilities on the second set of branches when items are not replaced.

mistakes.r: Multiply along the branches for AND; add the probabilities of different outcomes for OR.
mistakes.w: Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying.

mistakes.r: Different paths that satisfy the question are mutually exclusive: add them.
mistakes.w: Multiplying the outcome probabilities together when the question says "or".

mistakes.r: Branches leaving a node must account for all outcomes, so they add to exactly 1.
mistakes.w: Branch probabilities at a node that do not sum to 1 (for example 3/5 and 1/5).

mistakes.r: Every first-stage end needs a full set of second-stage branches.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to draw second-stage branches from every first-stage branch.

mistakes.r: Use P(at least one) = 1 − P(none), or list every path with at least one.
mistakes.w: Finding P(at least one) by adding some paths and missing one.

mistakes.r: Reversing the condition needs P(rain and late) ÷ P(late) = 0.12 ÷ 0.19 = 12/19.
mistakes.w: Using P(late | rain) = 0.4 when asked for P(rain | late).

mistakes.r: The denominator is the total probability of the given event, found by adding every path that ends in it.
mistakes.w: Using the first-stage probability as the denominator for a conditional probability.

mistakes.r: Show each product (for example 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20) so method marks can be awarded.
mistakes.w: Not showing the multiplication in working and only giving a final answer.

summary: You must be able to draw and complete tree diagrams for independent and dependent events (with and without replacement), multiply along branches for AND, add outcomes for OR, and use trees to calculate conditional probabilities such as P(A | B) at Higher tier. It matters because tree diagrams appear in most Edexcel probability questions and often carry 4 to 6 marks.

terms.d: A diagram with branches that shows all the possible outcomes of successive events and the probability of each branch.
One of the successive events in a tree diagram, for example the first pick or the second pick.
A line in a tree diagram representing one possible outcome of a stage, labelled with its probability.
The result at the end of a complete path through the tree, for example RB (red then blue).
Events where the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
Events where the outcome of the first does affect the probability of the second, for example selection without replacement.
Selection in which each item is put back before the next is chosen, so the probabilities do not change.
Selection in which items are not put back, so the number of items and the probabilities change.
The probability of an event given that another event has occurred, written P(B | A).
To find the probability of a sequence of events, multiply the probabilities along the branches.
To find the probability of one of several mutually exclusive outcomes, add their probabilities.
Events that cannot happen at the same time, so the probability of either is the sum of their probabilities.
The event not happening: P(A') = 1 − P(A). Used for at least one questions: 1 − P(none).
A tree diagram showing the numbers (frequencies) of items in each category instead of probabilities.
The probability of an event multiplied by the number of trials; an average, not a guarantee.
Events that between them cover every possible outcome, so their probabilities add to 1.

worked.q: (4 marks) A bag contains 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. Two counters are taken at random without replacement. (a) Work out the probability that both counters are the same colour. (b) Work out the probability that at least one counter is red.
steps: First pick: P(R) = 3/5, P(B) = 2/5. After R: 2 red, 2 blue left, so P(R) = 2/4, P(B) = 2/4. After B: 3 red, 1 blue left, so P(R) = 3/4, P(B) = 1/4.
(a) Same colour means RR or BB. P(RR) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20. P(BB) = 2/5 × 1/4 = 2/20.
(b) At least one red = 1 − P(no red) = 1 − P(BB) = 1 − 2/20 = 18/20 = 9/10.

worked.q: (4 marks) The probability that it rains on a day is 0.3. If it rains, the probability that Sam is late is 0.4. If it does not rain, the probability that Sam is late is 0.1. Given that Sam is late, work out the probability that it rained. Give your answer as a fraction.
steps: Rain and late: 0.3 × 0.4 = 0.12. Dry and late: 0.7 × 0.1 = 0.07.
P(rain | late) = P(rain and late) ÷ P(late) = 0.12 ÷ 0.19 = 12/19.

worked.q: (3 marks) A box holds 8 chocolates: 5 milk and 3 dark. Sofia takes three chocolates at random without replacement. (a) Work out the probability that all three are milk. (b) Work out the probability that at least one is dark.
steps: (b) P(at least one dark) = 1 − P(all milk) = 1 − 5/28 = 23/28.
